relationship_to_restored_text: Interpretive contemplative layer aligned by verse. This does not replace the source-audited restored translation.

verses.mystical_translation: A queen crosses distance not to flatter but to test celebrated wisdom with hard questions.
She arrives with her own wealth, people, and questions, speaking everything upon her heart.
Solomon meets the intellectual challenge without hiding from any subject.
She examines wisdom alongside the architecture it has produced.
Table, servants, clothing, ritual, and movement reveal a whole system of ordered abundance that takes away her breath.
She confirms that the report from afar carried truth.
Direct encounter exceeds reputation.
She notices those who stand near wisdom, though their labor and freedom remain questions.
Her blessing names the purpose of the throne: justice and righteousness for a beloved people.
She gives from her own royal abundance rather than appearing as a dependent admirer.
Ophir's fleet brings rare wood and stones beside gold.
Distant trees become temple supports and instruments of song.
The exchange remains reciprocal, and the queen returns to her own land with her servants.
Then the story weighs the gold that flows to Solomon in a single year.
Merchants, regional kings, and governors feed the accumulation.
Gold becomes shields too precious for ordinary defense.
More shields fill the palace forest as stored spectacle.
Ivory and gold turn animal death and mineral extraction into a throne.
Lions guard the seat through carved royal symbolism.
Twelve more lions make the staircase unlike any other kingdom.
Gold fills the cups while silver becomes beneath notice.
Ships return with precious metals, tusks, and captured animals from distant worlds.
The narrator crowns Solomon in both wealth and wisdom.
The world seeks his face to hear what was placed in his heart.
The annual pilgrimage brings gifts that also resemble tribute.
Chariots and horsemen multiply beneath the wise king.
Silver and cedar become common at the center because resources have been drawn there.
Egyptian and Anatolian horse markets feed the royal military system.
Solomon's merchants become arms brokers for neighboring kings.

contemplative_note: The queen's sentence is the chapter's measuring rod: a ruler exists to do justice and righteousness. Everything that follows—gold, ivory, captive animals, luxury, tribute, horses, and weapons—must answer to that standard.
